item.title: Is Psychotherapy Sustainable in the Internet Age?
item.description:
Therapy

Is Psychotherapy Sustainable in the Internet Age?

Personal Perspective: The right website may justify us or make us blame others.

Posted October 18, 2026

Key points
  • Psychotherapy needs a cultural context that allows for admitting something might be wrong.
  • The internet enables everyone to find communities where their behavior is affirmed, not challenged.
  • Modern culture's moralizing hinders therapeutic neutrality and honest exploration of inner conflict.

Every treatment requires a cultural context that will sustain it. For example, for a very long time, doctors could not practice medicine in a culture that forbade patients from taking off their clothes. Similarly, the intimacy in real psychotherapy is forbidden in many subcultures.

Many people live in situations that prevent them from attending regular appointments. It was certainly a great advance in mental health care when psychologists started thinking about what can be accomplished given the patient’s life constraints rather than always starting a therapy they knew couldn’t last (Horowitz et al., 1984). It was not an advance in psychotherapy, however, to insist that the few sessions being offered were as good as the ideal, open-ended treatment (Nordmo et al., 2020).

Core Factors for Success in Psychotherapy

The psychotherapy outcome literature has long settled the debate over what helps in psychotherapy (Norcross & Lambert, 2019). The problem is that there is no way to monetize these findings with new-sounding acronyms. Successful therapy needs a mutual understanding of what’s wrong with the patient, and a mutual agreement that the cause is psychological—typically, a pattern of behavior or expectations that were once adaptive and are now maladaptive. There must be a mutual, sensible understanding of how therapy can help—typically, with a case formulation that highlights the way patients treat themselves and the utility of bringing all the selves (or all the interpersonal response repertoires) into the therapy by speaking freely. (If the problem is the way other people treat the patient, then those other people must be included in the therapy.) Finally, relational bonds must be nurtured and maintained—bonds of the collaborative sort, not of some other sort such as nurturance, cheerleading, or preaching.

The analogy to physical therapy helps here. If you want to get in shape, improve your athletic performance, or live longer, consult a trainer, coach, or instructor. If there’s something wrong, consult a physical therapist.

The contemporary culture in many parts of America forbids concluding that there is something wrong with the patient. Instead, everyone is perfect in their own way. This attitude is promoted by an internet that will offer every person an online community in which their behavior is normative. Psychotherapy requires an understanding that the patient must adapt to reality; the internet readily adapts to the person.

Changes in Therapist Training and Identity-Based Approaches

Training programs at one time emphasized what was wrong with the student—what psychological patterns and expectations kept the student from fulfilling the demands of the role of therapist. This idea has become so toxic in many graduate programs that they no longer construe the students as needing to be trained (except in record-keeping). The only de facto requirement is that the therapist should once have suffered as the patient has. A patient with some identity element or some sort of pain doesn’t need a well-trained therapist; they need a therapist with the same identity element or the same sort of pain. The analogy to seeking an internet community that avoids rather than resolves conflict is obvious.

In a culture that moralizes as much as ours does, therapeutic neutrality reads as complicity with injustice rather than as offering a place to resolve internal conflict. The very idea of internal conflict seems counter-revolutionary. Therapists are pressured by the culture to stand up against injustice, even when the injustice is perpetrated by patients against themselves. The popular culture is currently bent towards victory over peaceful resolution between parties in conflict, and this extends to the psychology of the patient, where it is currently not only unfashionable but also fascistic to suggest that the part of the person who hates himself and the part of the person who is hated can learn to get along.

The patient’s task in psychotherapy is to take off the social mask and reveal what lies beneath. The therapist’s task is to create a space where it is sensible to do so. Neither of these is possible in a culture that insists that both parties immediately denounce every injustice. Instead, therapy in such a culture teaches the patient to adopt a new social mask, one of moral purity. In that way, we are as puritanical about politically incorrect impulses, feelings, and fantasies as the Victorians in Freud’s day were about sex.

Effects of Anti-Patriarchal Attitudes and Expertise in Therapy

Finally, it is impossible to create a collaborative alliance around working together in a culture that treats all frustration of the patient as patriarchal—and further insists that all patriarchy be denounced. Before the internet undermined expertise by making everyone with a phone feel like an expert, therapists were expected to be experts in psychology and in psychotherapy. Nowadays, claiming expertise is suspiciously patriarchal. The cure for suffering that was caused by mishandled power differentials is not to avoid all power differentials; it’s to get involved in power differentials that are not mishandled. This is not possible in a culture that assumes that all power differentials are evil.

My new novel, The Last Therapist, explores the challenges of providing psychotherapy in a culture of righteous purity and fear of acknowledging internal conflict.

item.title: Coping Meaningfully With Election Angst and Distress
item.description:
Career

Coping Meaningfully With Election Angst and Distress

How to face election hypersensitivity.

Posted October 18, 2026

Key points
  • Democracy and democratically-designed political systems are inherently messy and unpredictable.
  • Expect both existential angst and emotional distress when participating in electoral politics.
  • There is meaning to be found in each stage of the election process.
Source: Teacher Photo/Shutterstock

Since their beginning in ancient Greece, popularly referred to as the "birthplace of democracy," elections have been a key feature of political systems based on democratic principles. In this regard, there are some key elections that will take place in the near future, including the midterms in the United States next month and several national elections in Europe scheduled for early next year.

As someone with longstanding experience in the management of election campaigns,1 I’ve noticed a significant shift in how constituents perceive and, importantly, how they respond to the electoral process.

Both voters and nonvoters are increasingly suspicious of what they see—or think they see—happening in the political arena, making the perception of election integrity a formidable challenge. The lack of transparency of what takes place before an election, what happens when ballots are cast, and what occurs afterward when votes are tallied wreak havoc on public trust and confidence in the electoral process. All this can be fodder for triggering existential angst and/or emotional distress.

Global Political Polarization and Its Impact on Elections

On a global scale, we are living in an age of extreme political polarization and ideological discord. Recent political realignments and partisan conflicts worldwide, as well as armed conflicts and military action/wars, only serve to exacerbate an already tense election landscape. Leading up to the midterm elections in the U.S., there have been numerous reports of not only verbal abuse but also threats and acts of violence against candidates and their supporters. To be sure, such actions are unacceptable in a civil society.

Heightened tensions, of course, don’t just happen during the pre-election phase of this process; they can also be observed during the tabulation of voting results as well as during the post-election period, especially if your preferred candidate(s) is/are not elected. Compounded by feelings of political inefficacy (“my vote doesn’t count”; “the election has been stolen”), citizens can also become politically alienated and, as a result, more apathetic, frustrated, or angry with their government and public officials.

Elections provide us with important opportunities to learn and grow from our experience, as well as to discover meaning through the lens of politics; that is, as long as we assume personal and collective responsibility for the integrity of both the process and results. Without such responsibility, there can be no democracy, no real freedom.

Coping With Electoral Loss and Maintaining Faith in Democracy

Regardless of the type of election involved, there will always be winners and losers. Being on the losing side of an election need not create distrust in the electoral system, nor should it lead to giving up hope on the inherent value of democracy and the aspirational values upon which democratic political systems are based. Accepting loss is part of life, part of recognizing what you can control and what you can’t.

Drawing upon insights from existential philosophy and humanistic psychology, there are strategies that can be used in response to any pre-, during-, or post-election distress, anxiety, or even depression that may ensue.

The wisdom of psychiatrist, existential philosopher, and Holocaust survivor Viktor Frankl, author of Man’s Search for Meaning, can shine some light on this matter from a uniquely meaning-centric perspective.2 With his System of Logotherapy and Existential Analysis, Frankl offers guidance to advance the human quest for meaning in everyday life and work, including situations that may be unavoidable.

Among the most well-known tenets of Frankl’s humanistic approach is the notion of freedom of will: “Everything can be taken from a man but… the last of the human freedoms—to choose one’s attitude in any given set of circumstances, to choose one’s way.” In all situations, no matter how desperate or challenging they may appear or actually be, we always have the ultimate freedom to choose our attitude.

Of course, some individuals cope more easily than others with changes in circumstances, including times of disappointment, such as losing an election. As Frankl wisely advised, when we are no longer able to change a situation, we are challenged to change ourselves.

Core Principles for Coping With Election-Related Stress

Frankl’s meaning-centric approach includes a number of core principles that are described in some detail in our book, Prisoners of Our Thoughts.3 I’ve already introduced one of them, “Exercise the freedom to choose your attitude.” Here are some other principles that can offer guidance when coping with the stresses resulting from the outcomes, be they favorable or not, of the electoral process.

Detect the meaning of life’s moments. Observing and participating in political campaigns provide many opportunities for personal reflection. If done authentically, the exercise can help you discover deeper meaning in your experience, as well as increase your level of resilience and coping skills when dealing with stressful situations like those found during the election process.

Don’t work against yourself. Avoid becoming so fixated on an intent or outcome that you actually work against the desired result. In the political arena, a fixation on or obsession with a particular candidate for elected office can actually work against us, albeit subconsciously, if we are not mindful of our attitude and actions.4

Look at yourself from a distance. Since only human beings possess the capacity to look at themselves from a distance, you have the resilience-building option of viewing the situation at hand with a sense of perspective, even with a sense of humor, in order to ensure that you don’t become imprisoned by your thoughts and allow the situation to effectively crush your spirit.

Shift your focus of attention. To find the deeper meaning of any given problem or life challenge, deflect your attention from the situation at hand to something else, preferably to something positive, in order to build your coping mechanisms for dealing with stress and change. Limiting exposure to political news can help you focus on healthy living and restore your energy. Give yourself breaks from the news, especially politics, and limit your time on social media, which can intensify anxiety and depression, if you are unable to disconnect completely.

Every election can trigger existential angst and mental distress for some people, especially after electoral loss. To make matters worse, post-election emotional responses, both positive and negative, are intensified in a climate of contentious political divide and strife. It is my hope that some of the strategies presented in this post can help you reflect upon how you might more effectively cope with and address your own emotional response.
